reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this work the authors analyse how cells deal with the deregulated licensing of origins of replication caused by the
depletion of Geminin. Unlike previous studies, where defective licensing was driving large amounts of re-replication in
cancer cells, this study focuses on milder levels of DNA re-replication seen in immortalised cells, such as hTERT-RPE1
cells.
Through an siRNA screen, the authors identify FANCD2 as key in suppressing DNA damage and supporting cell
proliferation upon Geminin depletion. They then show that FANCD2 loss causes faster fork speed and accumulation of S1-
nuclease sensitive stretches of DNA, likely ssDNA gaps. Genomic analysis reveals that in Geminin depleted cells, FANCD2
is not only at difficult and late replicating DNA regions, but it is also seen at early replicating regions, in the proximity of
highly transcribed genes and clusters of early firing replication origins.
Surprisingly they find that dampening of transcription or R-loops digestion significantly supresses DNA damage in Geminin
depleted cells.
This study suggests a new mechanism for the generation of genomic instability upon reactivation of replication origins within
the same cell cycle, which now directly implicates transcription and collision between the “re-replication” and the
transcription machineries. Such a mechanism is likely to occur in pre-malignant cells leading to tumorigenesis.
The experiments are well performed and controlled, combining both classical cell biology and genomics approaches; the
results are clear-cut and important. The manuscript is well written and easy to read.
This reviewer has few minor comments that may improve the manuscript:
1. In supplementary Fig S1, it would be nice to show the efficiency of the co-depletion of Geminin and CDT1by western blot
and assess if CDT1 and CDT1+Geminin depleted cells are still efficiently replicating their DNA under these experimental
conditions.
2. In many instances nuclear area is used as surrogate for re-replication. I understand that such approach may not be
particularly sensitive, thus creating some confusion when the authors argue that geminin depletion has sometime “mild” or
“no” effects in immortalised cells. How does this assay compare to classical DNA content measurement by flow cytometry or
other techniques?
3. Please provide legends for Supplementary tables 1 and 2
4. The siRNA screen appears to also identify proteins that, when depleted, cause DNA damage which is prevented by
geminin depletion e.g. PLK3, NEK1, CDK7 and few others. If this is correct, can the authors mention and discuss it?
5. Fig 3C: does siFANCD2 increases fork speed compared to siCtrl?
6. Line 211 and Fig S3c-d: it is not clear why low doses of ATR inhibitors suppress re-replication. It is known that ATR
inhibition facilitates origin activation, thus I would expect the opposite phenotype. Is this a dose-dependent effect and is it
related to the override of mitotic checkpoint thus not leaving sufficient time for large quantities of DNA to accumulate? (see
also point 2 related to sensitivity of the nuclear area assay).
7. Line 337: how effective is Cordycepin in inhibiting general transcription and. in particular. in inhibiting transcription of the
genes located in the proximity of clusters of early firing origins?
8. Similarly, would Cordycepin treatment or RNAse1 overexpression also suppress FANCD2 binding at siGEMNN specific
peaks determined in fig 6b?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Initiation of eukaryotic DNA replication is tightly controlled and coordinated with cell cycle progression to ensure only a
single round of DNA synthesis. In metazoa this occurs primarily through careful regulation of CDT1 and Geminin levels.
Defective regulation of CDT1/Geminin can lead to re-replication of the genome which is mutagenic, toxic, and is implicated
in oncogenesis. However, the exact molecular consequences of CDT1/Geminin dysregulation are unclear. Badra-Fajardo et
al have investigated the consequences of Geminin dysregulation and identified an important role for FANCD2 in preserving
genome stability. They find that loss of FANCD2 causes DNA damage, chromosomal aberrations, and possibly cell death in
Geminin-deficient cells. Mechanistically, these consequences are proposed to arise from accumulation of single-stranded
DNA gaps and formation of DNA breaks that are a downstream consequence of re-replication. Furthermore, these effects
may be unequally distributed throughout the genome. Overall the authors have connected FANCD2 to defects in Geminin
function but there are major concerns about the mechanism proposed, the interpretation of the data, and the overall novelty
of FANCD2 function supported by the data.
Major concerns
1. The manuscript seems to imply a unique role for FANCD2 in responding to Geminin loss. However, the upstream
(FANCA in Fig 5) and downstream (RAD51, BRCA1, BRCA2 in Fig 1) components of the Fanconi Anemia pathway behave
similarly. It would thus seem that the role described for FANCD2 here reflects the Fanconi Anemia pathway’s function and
not something more unique about FANCD2. Because a major role of the FA pathway is to coordinate DNA breaks in a
controlled manner (by XPF-ERCC1) this would seem to contradict the model that FANCD2 is preventing breaks. The data
would certainly support a model that FANCD2 prevents break accumulation, but not that it prevents break formation.
2. It is well established that cancerous cells are much more readily undergo re-replication following Geminin/CDT1
dysregulation. hTERT-RPE1 cells are examined in Figure 1 but the remainder of the manuscript focuses on cancerous cells
(U2OS, MCF7, 293T, HCT116). It’s unclear how much of the observed effects are specific to cancerous cells.
3. The manuscript focuses on re-replication but this is only directly measured once (Fig. S1A). For the remainder of the
manuscript, nuclear size is used as a proxy. Not only is nuclear size very indirect but it is unclear whether it serves a
reasonable proxy: in Fig S1A the fraction of cells that exhibit increased nuclear area is much greater than the fraction of cells
that exhibit >4n DNA content. The lack of direct measurements of re-replication and concerns about the suitability of cell size
as a proxy for re-replication call into question most of the authors’ conclusions that relate to re-replication.
4. Geminin knockdown is likely to have effects other than re-replication of the genome. The mechanism of re-replication by
geminin is loading of additional MCM complexes followed by origin firing on the already-replicated DNA. There is no reason
this could not also occur in the unreplicated region of the genome, which could manifest as unscheduled/excess origin firing
and may account for some of the effects observed (e.g. PMID29466339). Taken together with point (1), above, it seems very
possible the authors are documenting breaks induced by replication-transcription collisions and repaired by the Fanconi
Anemia pathway.
5. The is an ~24 hour delay between FANCD2 and gamma H2AX focus formation (Fig. 3A). Because the cell cycle in U2OS
cells (used in Fig 3A) is approximately 24 hours it would seem very unlikely that the FANCD2 levels and damage are both
occurring within S phase or G2, as would seem to be implied by the model that FANCD2 protects forks from excessive
breakage. The H2AX foci would at the very least need to arise from the following S phase, but the simpler explanation would
be that they arise from breaks during mitosis.
6. In several figures the authors report increased number of foci of different DNA damage response proteins following
Geminin knockdown (Figs 1c, 2d, 3a, 4a, 4d, 5a, 5d, 7d-e). Because Geminin increases nuclear area there would be
expected to be some increase in foci per nucleus independent of any effects on DNA damage. The same issue may also be
true for nuclear signal intensity (depending on how it was calculated). As the data stands, many of the increases in foci (and
possibility nuclear signal) could be a consequence of increased nuclear size.
7. Similar to the concerns about nuclear size, re-replication is expected to result in more DNA per nucleus and thus an
increase in replication proteins on DNA (E.g. RPA in Fig 4A-B). The same would also be true for DNA damage foci because
more replication would increase the level of spontaneous DNA damage. It is thus not clear how meaningful increased DNA
replication/repair foci are under conditions where re-replication may be taking place.
8. The genome wide distribution of FANCD2 presented in Figure 6 may not be particularly meaningful because there is no
correction for the prevalence of different genomic features. For example, the prevalence of FANCD2 peaks at intergenic
regions and introns in Fig 6E could simply be because this constitutes most of the genome. Similarly, the approximately 50%
overlap between FANCD2-bound genes in Fig. 6D is very similar to what would be expected for any two randomly selected
sets of genes. As things stand, many of the conclusions drawn from genomic analysis may not be meaningful.
9. The effects of Geminin and FANCD2 knockdown on cell survival seem to be purely additive (Fig. 1D), in contrast to the
effects on the DNA damage response which are clearly synergistic (Fig. 1C). The DNA damage data fit with the authors’
model of FANCD2 responding to Geminin knockdown but the viability data do not. It is not clear whether Fig 1D supports a
role for the authors’ proposed mechanism in ensuring cell viability.
Minor concerns
10. The legend for Figure 1 refers to panel c but appears to actually be referring to b.
11. For Figure 2A it is not obvious that Geminin knockdown causes increased FANCD2 recruitment to chromatin. The
difference is modest and total cellular FANCD2 is increased so the increased binding could just reflect higher protein levels.
12. It is unclear what the asterisk in Fig 2C corresponds to.
13. The analysis of Cbio data in Fig. 2E cannot be used to draw a causal conclusion because this data only demonstrates
correlation. Also it is unclear how this analysis constitutes n=3 as the legend would seem to indicate.
14. When discussing Figure 5 the authors conclude that Geminin loss “promotes activation of canonical FA signaling and
recruitment of monoubiquitinated FANCD2”. They did demonstrate a role for FANCA following Geminin knockdown and can
infer importance of the FA pathway following Geminin knockdown, but they cannot infer any altered signaling (especially
because they did not measure signaling).
15. For Fig 7d-e how do the authors know that the RPA signal is due to gaps and not single-stranded DNA arising directly
from R-loops?
16. In the results section, the authors state “Finally, we tested whether increased formation of ssDNA gaps in Geminin and
FANCD2 double-depleted cells would result in chromosome fragility and high levels of genomic instability.” There is no
direct measurement of gaps and the intervention (Geminin depletion) is highly indirect so they cannot make this conclusion.
17. For Fig S1A the graphs of cell counts should be labeled to indicate which is control vs which is Geminin depleted

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
FANCD2 restrains fork progression and prevents fragility at early replicating origins upon re-replication
We sincerely thank the reviewers for the detailed evaluation of our manuscript. The
insightful and encouraging comments helped us to perform additional experiments and
a thorough revision of the manuscript. In this response letter, we address the reviewers’
comments point-by-point and outline the revisions we have made to enhance the quality
and clarity of our study.
Point-by-point response to the reviewers’ comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Major Comments:
1.The main approach in the study to measure re-replication is nuclear area
measurements. Re-replication is associated with increased origin firing. While the
authors do perform DNA fiber studies, there is no mention of % initiation or inter origin
distance which is very peculiar. This needs to be addressed.
We thank the reviewer for this consideration and agree that analyzing the percentage of
origin firing was an important question to address in the context of aberrant DNA
licensing. In the revised manuscript, we included the percentage of origin firing in respect
to the total replicative structures of DNA fibers obtained for each condition. The analysis
of three replicates shows that Geminin depletion slightly increases the rate of origin
initiation, although this increase is not further enhanced by FANCD2 loss (see new Fig.
3e). Thus, we believe that although Geminin loss might promote some activation of
dormant origins as a consequence of aberrant CDT1 activity and/or to counteract the
perturbations on replication -especially as cells undergo prolonged re-replication-
FANCD2 primarily functions in reducing the progression rate of re-replicating forks rather
than directly controlling origin firing. These observations are in line with the idea that re-
replication occurs primarily at constitutive origins that are used during normal replication,
which also tend to be early replicating1 where we indeed observe an accumulation of
FANCD2 (see Fig. 6). These results are included and further discussed in the submitted
revised manuscript (page 8).
2.It is unclear why authors haven’t assessed copy number changes that are very
indicative of re-replication by sequencing or DNA microarrays. In addition, re-replication
can cause aneuploidy which is easy to detect and report.
We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern and agree that another approach to measure
re-replication was important to strengthen our results. Although examining copy number
changes is an interesting metric, these changes have only been observed upon massive
levels of re-replication2,3. Geminin depletion typically induces partial re-replication and
cell to cell heterogeneity, making it difficult to observe such differences by accounting for
net copy number changes. As for aneuploidy, this metric requires that cells pass through
mitosis, however origin re-licensing after Geminin depletion activates checkpoint
signaling and promotes cell arrest in G2/M, which indeed we show is required for
extensive re-replication. This, together with the fact that U2OS cells already present
extensive levels of aneuploidy4, made it difficult to use this assay to quantify levels of re-
replication.
As an alternative and following the reviewers suggestions (including reviewer #1 in major
point number 5), we implemented flow cytometry analyses in U2OS and hTERT-RPE1
cells depleted of Geminin at different timepoints to examine the kinetics of the cell cycle
and the prevalence of cells with DNA content above G2/M cells incorporating EdU
as a metric of re-replication. Our analyses in U2OS cells show that Geminin depletion
induces an initial accumulation of cells in S phase at 24 hs, while there is already a small
proportion of cells over-replicating (>4 C) when compared to control cells (New
Supplementary Fig. 1a). However, the high prevalence of cells with DNA content above
G2/M levels occurs at 48 hs, where about 30% of cells are re-replicating, consistent with
the results observed by measuring nuclear areas (New Supplementary Fig. 1b) and
reinforcing this timepoint as the appropriate for the remainder of the study. As expected,
there were no evident signs of re-replication in hTERT-RPE1 cells depleted of Geminin
(New Supplementary Fig. 1e, f). Importantly, in the revised manuscript we also included
a new set of experiments using this approach to show the effect of depleting FANCD2 in
re-replicating cells. According to the results obtained by measuring the nuclear areas,
depletion of FANCD2 did not increase the levels of re-replication but rather slightly
reduced them (New Fig. 3c). We provide cell cycle distributions for each timepoint and
cell line from 3 independent experiments together with gates applied in the Source data.
3.Does Geminin loss or co-depletion with FANCD2 induce cell death? This needs to be
addressed.
We thank the reviewer for this comment, and we are glad to further clarify the results
from our work. Throughout the study, we performed clonogenic assays to focus on the
long-term proliferative potential of re-replicating cells, either in cells solely depleted of
Geminin, or upon double silencing of Geminin and FANCD2 or the alternative targets
indicated in each case (see New Fig. 1d, New Supplementary Fig. 2b, d and e, New
Supplementary Fig. 3, New Fig. 4, New Fig. 5c, f and New Supplementary Fig. 5f). Rather
than survival assays -usually employed to reveal acute cytotoxicity at a short time
intervals- we conducted clonogenic assays, as this approach can capture the ability of
individual cells to proliferate and form colonies over longer periods5-8. As we describe in
the results section, our analyses show that depletion of Geminin slightly reduces cell
survival in normal cells (New Fig. 1d, while this effect is significantly more acute in cancer
cells (New Supplementary Fig. 2b, d and e). Co-depletion FANCD2 renders Geminin-
depleted cells hypersensitive across cell lines (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2). Cell
death is not detected at early time points, when our analysis of molecular pathways takes
place, by either cytometry analyses (sub G1 population, New Supplementary Fig. 1 and
New Fig. 3), cell counts or MTT (data not shown). This rules out apoptotic pathways as
the cause of the observed molecular phenotypes.
4.The entire manuscript hinges on one molecular approach, siRNA mediated transient
depletion to study the role of Geminin in re-replication. An alternate approach to inhibit
such as the small molecule inhibitor targeting CDT1/Geminin protein complex (PMID:
35548337) and CRISPR to stably knockdown Geminin and(or) CDT1 is required to
strengthen the findings.
In our initial submission, we compared the effect on cell survival of siRNA-mediated
depletion of Geminin across different cells lines, but we additionally used an auxin-
inducible degron system integrated in HCT116 cells for the rapid degradation of Geminin
and observed increased sensitivity to silencing of FANCD2 (New Supplementary Fig.
2e). We performed additional analyses in these cells by quantifying the proportion of cells
with FANCD2 foci or γH2AX nuclear intensities. Geminin depletion alone elicits very high
levels of DNA damage in this system (Fig. R1a). This makes the detection of even higher
γH2AX levels by co-depletion of FANCD2 technically challenging (Fig. R1b). We provide
these data, which are consistent with our findings, below. To further strengthen our
results, during the revision period we generated a stable U2OS cell line containing a
doxycycline (dox)-dependent inducible short hairpin (shRNA) targeting human Geminin.
In the revised version of this manuscript, we included a new set of data using this system
and validating the increased sensitivity of Geminin-depleted cells to loss of FANCD2 in
terms of DNA damage and cell survival (New Supplementary Fig. 2c, d).

We understand that the potential confusion might have arisen mainly due to the fact that

from the flow cytometry analysis using EdU and PI, which reveals a distinct cell
population exhibiting >4C DNA content and high levels of EdU incorporation
(Supplementary Fig. 1a), which we identify and refer to as re-replicating cells for the
remainder of the manuscript. Additionally, we tried to re-structure the results included in
the study to thoroughly address the potential ambiguity regarding the characteristics of
re-replicating cells.

measure cell survival without interfering with the fluorescent markers. As an alternative
and since we plated the same number of cells per well, for the screening we used cell
counts as a preliminary measure of viability. We validated the robustness of this metric
in small-scale pilot screens by transfecting the cells with cell death-siRNA controls or
with CDT2, which causes massive re-replication (New Supplementary Table 1 and New
Supplementary Table 2). Consistently, the screening data also showed reduced cell
counts when using these controls or after silencing essential genes such as PLK1 or
cyclin D (New Supplementary Table 1 and New Supplementary Table 2). As mentioned
previously, for subsequent analyses we employed clonogenic assays to assess the long-

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment, which allowed us to clarify this point. As the
reviewer correctly noted, both IdU- and CldU-labeled fibers are indeed of the same

sister forks emanating from the same origin. Replication forks exhibit asymmetry under
replication stress (endogenous or exogenous)10,11. In our case, our data indicate that this
asymmetry is linked to the replication stress arising from uncontrolled progression of
replicating forks in the absence of Geminin and FANCD2. We believe these points are
now clear in the revised manuscript. As requested by the reviewer, the raw data

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this work the authors analyse how cells deal with the deregulated licensing of origins
of replication caused by the depletion of Geminin. Unlike previous studies, where
defective licensing was driving large amounts of re-replication in cancer cells, this study
focuses on milder levels of DNA re-replication seen in immortalised cells, such as
hTERT-RPE1 cells.
Through an siRNA screen, the authors identify FANCD2 as key in suppressing DNA
damage and supporting cell proliferation upon Geminin depletion. They then show that
FANCD2 loss causes faster fork speed and accumulation of S1-nuclease sensitive
stretches of DNA, likely ssDNA gaps. Genomic analysis reveals that in Geminin depleted
cells, FANCD2 is not only at difficult and late replicating DNA regions, but it is also seen
at early replicating regions, in the proximity of highly transcribed genes and clusters of
early firing replication origins.
Surprisingly they find that dampening of transcription or R-loops digestion significantly
supresses DNA damage in Geminin depleted cells.
This study suggests a new mechanism for the generation of genomic instability upon
reactivation of replication origins within the same cell cycle, which now directly implicates
transcription and collision between the “re-replication” and the transcription machineries.
Such a mechanism is likely to occur in pre-malignant cells leading to tumorigenesis.
The experiments are well performed and controlled, combining both classical cell biology
and genomics approaches; the results are clear-cut and important. The manuscript is
well written and easy to read.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Initiation of eukaryotic DNA replication is tightly controlled and coordinated with cell
cycle progression to ensure only a single round of DNA synthesis. In metazoa this
occurs primarily through careful regulation of CDT1 and Geminin levels. Defective
regulation of CDT1/Geminin can lead to re-replication of the genome which is
mutagenic, toxic, and is implicated in oncogenesis. However, the exact molecular
consequences of CDT1/Geminin dysregulation are unclear. Badra-Fajardo et al have
investigated the
consequences of Geminin dysregulation and identified an important role for FANCD2 in
preserving genome stability. They find that loss of FANCD2 causes DNA damage,
chromosomal aberrations, and possibly cell death in Geminin-deficient cells.
Mechanistically, these consequences are proposed to arise from accumulation of single-
stranded DNA gaps and formation of DNA breaks that are a downstream consequence
of re-replication. Furthermore, these effects may be unequally distributed throughout the
genome. Overall the authors have connected FANCD2 to defects in Geminin function
but there are major concerns about the mechanism proposed, the interpretation of the
data, and the overall novelty of FANCD2 function supported by the data.
Major concerns
1. The manuscript seems to imply a unique role for FANCD2 in responding to Geminin
loss. However, the upstream (FANCA in Fig 5) and downstream (RAD51, BRCA1,
BRCA2 in Fig 1) components of the Fanconi Anemia pathway behave similarly. It would
seem that the role described for FANCD2 here reflects the Fanconi Anemia pathway’s
function and not something more unique about FANCD2. Because a major role of the
FA pathway is to coordinate DNA breaks in a controlled manner (by XPF-ERCC1) this
would seem to contradict the model that FANCD2 is preventing breaks. The data
would certainly support a model that FANCD2 prevents break accumulation, but not
that it prevents break formation.
We would like to thank the reviewer for this comment. It is indeed correct that some repair
proteins, such as BRCA1/2, were found during our primary screen. However, we believe
that activation of these proteins after Geminin depletion, as it occurs with FANCD2, is
associated to their function during fork stability and not directly with inducing breaks in a
regulated fashion, as is the case upon inter-strand crosslinks. If the observed FANCD2
function during re-replication would be to promote DNA breaks (by XPF-ERCC1), we
would expect reduced DNA damage upon its depletion, which is not the case, as
observed by increased γH2AX or 53BP1 (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 2).
In the revised manuscript, we have performed a number of additional experiments to
reinforce our data showing FANCD2 recruitment prior to formation of DNA breaks. Along
with the kinetics of FANCD2 and γH2AX in Geminin-depleted cells (New Fig. 2c), we
included new results from a synchronization experiment in Geminin-depleted U2OS cells
(see New Fig. 2.d and New Supplementary Fig. 4b). During the synchronization, we
depleted Geminin to ensure S-phase entry with no Geminin expression, and then
released and subsequently monitored EdU incorporation, together with FANCD2 and
pH3, over a 30hs time course. Depletion of Geminin led to a time-dependent
accumulation of cells that were actively synthesizing DNA at the G2/M boundary (EdU
and pH3-double positive) (New Fig. 2d and New Supplementary Fig. 4b), sustaining the
idea that FANCD2 recruitment occurs early and precedes high levels of DNA breaks.
Additionally, to strengthen our results showing that FANCD2 binds to chromatin upon re-
replication at replication forks, in the revised manuscript we included a new set of data
employing the SIRF assay, which combines EdU labeling of nascent DNA with a
proximity ligation assay (PLA) to detect proteins at newly synthesized DNA9. Using this
approach, we observed a significant increase in the number of FANCD2-EdU interacting
foci following Geminin depletion (New Fig. 3a). These results were also validated through
the analysis of other replisome factors by PLA (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 4c),
which showed that this interaction is not only increased in S-phase cells but becomes
evident in G2-arrested cells (New Fig. 3b), thus confirming that FANCD2 is directly
recruited at forks upon re-replication. We hope that the reviewer will now agree that our
new data strongly support our initial conclusions of a direct function of FANCD2 in
protecting re-replicating forks.
2. It is well established that cancerous cells are much more readily undergo re-replication
following Geminin/CDT1 dysregulation. hTERT-RPE1 cells are examined in Figure 1 but
the remainder of the manuscript focuses on cancerous cells (U2OS, MCF7, 293T,
HCT116). It’s unclear how much of the observed effects are specific to cancerous cells.

address the molecular mechanism by which FANCD2 promotes the survival of re-
replicating cells. However, we have also provided validation of critical phenotypes in non-

4. Geminin knockdown is likely to have effects other than re-replication of the genome.
The mechanism of re-replication by geminin is loading of additional MCM complexes
followed by origin firing on the already-replicated DNA. There is no reason this could not
also occur in the unreplicated region of the genome, which could manifest as
unscheduled/excess origin firing and may account for some of the effects observed

authors are documenting breaks induced by replication-transcription collisions and
repaired by the Fanconi Anemia pathway.
As the reviewer rightly points out, ectopic licensing and thus recruitment of additional
MCMs in Geminin-depleted cells is likely to affect un-replicated regions of the genome
and increase transcription-replication collisions at those sites. Indeed, we performed
additional analysis and observed that Geminin loss increases origin firing (New Fig. 3e),
supporting that both re-firing as well as ectopic firing of origins take place when Geminin
is inhibited. According to these findings, we demonstrate that inhibiting active
transcription or eliminating R-loops alleviates the phenotypes exhibited in Geminin
depleted cells (Fig. 7d, e). However, as we discussed in comment number 1 to this
reviewer, our data strongly suggest that FANCD2 is not recruited following the break, but
at re-replicating forks as a mean of stabilizing and limiting fork progression and thus
protecting them from breaks. This idea is supported by the kinetics of FANCD2 and
γH2AX in Geminin-depleted cells (New Fig. 2c), together with the new set of experiments
in synchronized cells (New Fig. 2d) and those employing SIRF and PLA assays, in which
we observed a significant increase in the number of FANCD2-EdU, as well as PCNA-
FANCD2 and MCM2-FANCD2, interacting foci following Geminin depletion when
compared to controls (New Fig. 3a, b and Supplementary Fig. 4c).
5. The is an ~24 hour delay between FANCD2 and gamma H2AX focus formation (Fig.
3A). Because the cell cycle in U2OS cells (used in Fig 3A) is approximately 24 hours it

forks from excessive breakage. The H2AX foci would at the very least need to arise
from the following S phase, but the simpler explanation would be that they arise from
breaks during mitosis.
Our results show that, at least in the context of re-replication, DNA breaks do not arise
upon mitosis but rather accumulate extensively when re-replicating cells are arrested at
G2/M. These results are supported by the new set of data provided from flow cytometry
analysis of EdU and PI (see New Supplementary Fig. 1a) and synchronization
experiments (see New Fig. 2d); Geminin depletion induces an initial accumulation of
cells in S phase within 24hs, while there is a small proportion of cells over-replicating.
The accumulation of cells in S probably reflects the activation of an intra-S checkpoint
that slows cell cycle progression and limits the proportion of re-replicating cells. This is
consistent with an early detection of FANCD2 foci but not γH2AX during the kinetics
experiment (New Fig. 2c). Over time, we observe how re-replicating cells continue
accumulating at the G2/M boundary, showing a prevalence of about 30% of cells
exhibiting >4C DNA content after 48hs (New Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). Importantly, this
percentage highly fits with the proportion of cells showing increased nuclear area and
DNA breaks in the kinetics of FANCD2 and γH2AX for asynchronous cells (New Fig. 2c),

Fig. 4b) , as expected if cells re-replicate while being arrested at the G2/M. Consistently,
abrogation of the checkpoint, which is expected to lead to entry into mitosis, resulted in
decreased re-replication, reduced DNA damage and aberrant mitotic figures (New
Supplementary Fig. 5). These results support our model in which DNA break do not arise
from mitosis but from massive re-replication after cells arrest at G2/M.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

DNA replication is tightly regulated to ensure a single round of chromosome duplication per cell division. DNA licensing restricts origin firing to once-per-cell-cycle while aberrant licensing promotes re-replication and genome instability. Here, we investigate the mechanisms that protect genome integrity following re-replication induced by depletion of the licensing inhibitor Geminin. We find that re-replicating cells require FANCD2 to prevent genome instability. FANCD2 is rapidly recruited to chromatin upon Geminin loss, where it limits unrestrained fork progression and prevents single strand DNA gap accumulation and fork breakage. Genome-wide analyses reveal that upon re-replication, FANCD2 localizes to early origins within highly transcribed regions prone to accumulate R-loops and enriched in early replicating fragile sites. Importantly, reducing transcription and R-loops alleviates re-replication-induced genome fragility, whereas PARP inhibition exacerbates it. Our study uncovers a role for FANCD2 in safeguarding genome integrity during re-replication, offering avenues for selective targeting of cancer cells.

---

## Introduction

Accurate DNA duplication is essential during somatic cell division to ensure the inheritance of a complete copy of parental DNA by the offspring. In eukaryotes, replication initiates from discrete genomic regions known as origins, which are spatially distributed along the chromosome and become activated in clusters that follow a defined temporal program to achieve the complete replication of the genome1,2. Replication initiation is mediated by two major steps that are temporarily spaced by the different activity of cyclin-dependent kinases: origin licensing (helicase loading) in G1 and origin firing (helicase activation) in S-phase. Origin licensing refers to the assembly of pre-replicative complexes (pre-RCs) containing the origin recognition complex (ORC), CDC6 and CDT1, and the inactive form of the mini-chromosome maintenance 2–7 (MCM) helicase onto each origin of replication 3–7, whereas origin firing entails the recruitment of additional replication factors for the conversion of pre-RCs into active replisomes8–10. Uncoupling between licensing and firing is crucial to ensure that no genomic region is left un-replicated while limiting single origin firing to once per cell cycle11,12. Among all the licensing proteins involved in pre-RC formation, CDT1 undergoes the greatest control mechanisms as it recruits soluble replicative helicases from the nucleus to ORC and CDC6-bound origins13,14. Consistently, earlier work showed that aberrant CDT1 activity induces re-replication and DNA breakage across species. Over-expression of CDT1 in fission yeast cells leads to re-replication and gene amplification15. Accordingly, addition of CDT1 to X. laevis eggs or over-expression of the ortholog of CDT1 in Drosophila is sufficient to induce re-replication and DNA damage16,17. In mammalians, ectopic expression of CDT1 promotes re-replication and tumorigenesis18–22, and inhibition of its ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis has demonstrated to induce apoptosis in several cancer models23,24. Besides transcriptional control of CDT1 expression and fine-tuning over its activity through the ubiquitin proteasome system25, timely regulation of CDT1 depends on Geminin, a small protein only present in metazoans that acts as an inhibitor of pre-RC assembly by direct binding to CDT1 in S and G226–29. Control over DNA licensing by Geminin is considered a redundant mechanism in metazoa to prevent any non-degraded and nuclear-free CDT1 from initiating illegitimate licensing of origins outside of G1. According to this, Geminin loss induces re-replication and DNA damage selectively in cancer cells30,31, which usually exhibit an abnormal expression of several licensing factors and compromised tumor barriers32. These results are consistent with analysis in vivo, where Geminin ablation has demonstrated to favor tumorigenesis and induces cell death in neural stem cells during development33,34. The dependency of highly proliferative cells on Geminin could be a genomic trait of therapeutic significance in cancer, and small molecules phenocopying the effects of inhibiting Geminin activity are being currently characterized with promising results35,36. The increasing evidence suggesting that re-replication is a driving force of tumorigenesis argues for a better understanding of the mechanisms detecting and preventing re-replication associated DNA lesions.

Here, we show that cells depleted of Geminin require FANCD2 to promote cell survival and prevent deleterious levels of DNA damage. FANCD2 is pivotal during repair of inter-strand crosslinks (ICLs)37, but recent studies have demonstrated that it also plays a fundamental role during replication stress by promoting fork stability38. Our results indicate that Geminin depletion induces FANCD2 recruitment onto chromatin early during the first round of replication, which is required to limit the unrestrained progression of re-replicating forks. Consequently, loss of FANCD2 in Geminin-deficient cells triggers the accumulation of single strand DNA (ssDNA) gaps and leads to massive fork breakage, which ultimately results in increased genomic instability. Genome-wide analysis of FANCD2 distribution on chromatin upon Geminin depletion demonstrates its enrichment at early DNA origins localized within highly transcribed genes, which are characterized by increased levels of transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs) and DNA damage. The results in this study reveal a function of FANCD2 in the maintenance of genome stability upon re-replication and provide insights into the clinical potential of targeting Geminin in FA/BRCA-deficient cancers.

---

## Results

High-content screening identifies FANCD2 as essential to prevent DNA damage in Geminin-depleted cells
To identify mechanisms involved in the detection and repair of DNA lesions associated with aberrant licensing, we examined the effects of Geminin depletion on re-replication and DNA damage across different cell lines. We performed flow cytometry on Geminin-depleted and EdU pulse-labeled cells at different time points, which allowed us to measure the prevalence of cells with a DNA content greater than G2/M that were incorporating EdU as a metric for re-replication. As an alternative approach to quantify the levels of re-replication, we also measured nuclear areas39, while we analyzed γH2AX and 53BP1 signals as proxies of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Depletion of Geminin in U2OS cancer cells resulted in an initial accumulation of cells in S phase within the first 24 h, with a small proportion undergoing re-replication (>4C DNA content) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). A high prevalence of re-replicating cells was observed by 48 hs, at which point approximately 30% of cells showed >4C DNA content and active EdU incorporation (Supplementary Fig. 1a). These results were also reproduced by measuring nuclear areas (Supplementary Fig. 1b) and were also accompanied by a significant increase in γH2AX and 53BP1 signals (Supplementary Fig. 1c). Co-depletion of CDT1 partially suppressed these phenotypes (Supplementary Fig. 1d), indicating that these effects are dependent on active DNA replication. In contrast, depletion of Geminin in non-cancerous hTERT-RPE1 cells had minimal effects on re-replication and DNA damage (Supplementary Fig. 1e-g), supporting the notion that Geminin prevents re-replication selectively in cancer cells30,31. Accordingly, Geminin depletion increased DNA damage in MCF7 cancer cells but had a minor effect in the non-tumorigenic MCF10A cell line (Supplementary Fig. 1h).

The mild effects observed in hTERT-RPE1 cells 48 h after Geminin depletion provided an ideal system to achieve low-level re-replication and prompted us to employ this cell line to perform a high-content screening for factors required to maintain genome stability in cells primed for re-replication. To that end, we used a custom-designed siRNA library targeting 300 genes associated with the DNA damage response (DDR) and DNA repair pathways (Supplementary Data 1). After transient transfection with the siRNA library, control and Geminin-depleted hTERT-RPE1 cells were pulse-labelled with EdU for 1 h prior to fixation, and total cell counts, as well as EdU and γH2AX signal intensities, were measured as markers of cell viability and DNA damage (Fig. 1a).

The results of the screen yielded two distinct classes of candidates, consisting of genes whose depletion was toxic to both cell lines (Geminin-depleted and control), which served as a control to validate the methodology of the screening, and a second class, comprising genes whose depletion was particularly toxic to Geminin-depleted cells, which were identified as hits. As expected, among the top-scoring genes whose downregulation increased DNA damage and compromised survival of both Geminin-depleted and control cells, we identified critical regulators of the cell cycle and cell cycle-checkpoint pathways40–42 (i.e. PLK1, WEE1 or CHK1) (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 2). Concentrating on the candidates whose downregulation increased DNA damage or interfered with survival specifically in Geminin-depleted cells, we identified BRWD3, a histone reader and substrate of the Cullin 4-DDB1 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex43, and the pro-survival and BCL2-related protein BCL2L244 as top hits (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 2). Importantly, among the top candidates increasing DNA damage specifically in Geminin-depleted cells, we also found FANCD2 (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 2), a central component of the FA pathway traditionally associated with repair of ICLs37. Interestingly, other FA signaling components which cooperate with FANCD2 during ICL repair (such as BRCA1/2 or ERCC1) did not score positive in our screening (Supplementary Data 2), suggesting that the role of FANCD2 during re-replication is independent from its canonical ICL repair function. These results, together with the growing evidence supporting a critical role for FANCD2 in maintaining replication fork stability38, led us to prioritize this candidate for further analyses. Thus, we validated our results from the screening with a different set of siRNAs, which confirmed increased γH2AX intensities and 53BP1 foci (Fig. 1c) and revealed a significant reduction in long-term cell survival, as measured by clonogenic assays (Fig. 1d), in double Geminin and FANCD2 knockdowns when compared to control or single-depleted cells.

A similar effect was observed in cancer cells with high levels of re-replication. Specifically, this was confirmed in U2OS cells in which Geminin was depleted by siRNA or through a doxycycline-inducible shRNA (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b, and Supplementary Fig. 3a, b), as well as in HCT116 cells containing an auxin-inducible degron (AID)45 for total inactivation of Geminin (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Of note, co-depletion of Geminin and FANCD2 impaired long-term clonogenic survival but did not induce early apoptotic cell death, as demonstrated by analysis of Annexin V+-PI and cleaved Caspase-3 (Supplementary Fig. 2c, d). These results are in line with the limited effects observed in cell counts during the screen (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 2) and exclude the possibility that the effects are due to acute cytotoxicity.

Additionally, these results were further supported by assessing the effect of Geminin depletion in FANCD2-KO PD20 cells derived from a FA-D2 patient. As expected, silencing of Geminin induced significant levels of DSBs and reduced cell viability in PD20 cells (Supplementary Fig. 3d, e). Importantly, introduction of the corrected wild-type (WT) FANCD2 rescued these phenotypes to basal levels (Supplementary Fig. 3d, e), altogether suggesting that Geminin-depleted cells require FANCD2 to limit extensive DNA damage and promote cell survival.

FANCD2 is recruited at re-replicating forks prior to massive DNA breakage
To explore the potential contribution of FANCD2 in preventing DSBs during re-replication, we initially examined its localization on chromatin. Subcellular fractionation of U2OS cells depleted of Geminin revealed increased FANCD2 recruitment to chromatin (Fig. 2a). Consistently, Geminin depletion also induced the formation of FANCD2 foci, which localized near γH2AX sites (Fig. 2b). To determine whether FANCD2 activation is a general response to re-replication, we also analyzed the formation of FANCD2 foci following mild over-expression of CDT1. Since transient overexpression of this protein induces massive re-replication in cancer cells46, we generated a stable clone expressing a CDT1-GFP fusion integrated into the genome of hTERT-RPE1 cells. This clone exhibited cell cycle-regulated CDT1 expression at levels 2-3 times higher than endogenous CDT1, sufficient to induce DNA damage without massively altering re-replication, as demonstrated by analysis of γH2AX intensities and nuclear areas (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). As expected, over-expression of CDT1 in hTERT-RPE1 cells led to an increase in the proportion of cells with FANCD2 foci when compared to GFP-NLS control cells (Supplementary Fig. 4b), suggesting that FANCD2 is actively recruited to chromatin upon re-replication. Moreover, analysis of publicly available (TCGA) data (https://www.cbioportal.org) revealed an upregulation of FANCD2 in subgroups of bladder, uterine and breast cancers with high CDT1 expression (Supplementary Fig. 4c), consistent with an association of FANCD2 with aberrant DNA licensing.

Given that FANCD2 recruitment on chromatin is considered a consequence of replication fork blockage47–50, and our results in U2OS cells demonstrating an initial accumulation of cells in S prior to high levels of re-replication (Supplementary Fig. 1a), we hypothesized that Geminin depletion could trigger FANCD2 recruitment at stalled forks prior to the formation of widespread DSBs. To test this hypothesis, we measured the presence of FANCD2 foci and the increase in γH2AX nuclear intensities in Geminin-depleted U2OS cells in a time-course experiment. FANCD2 foci were observed as early as 12 h after siRNA transfection whereas γH2AX did not significantly accumulate until 48 h (Fig. 2c). Consistent with the analysis of FANCD2 foci, we did not observe a significant increase in the nuclear area until 12 h after transfection (Supplementary Fig. 5a), suggesting that upon Geminin depletion, FANCD2 recruitment on chromatin occurs early upon re-replication and precedes DNA breakage.

To further explore the dynamics of FANCD2 recruitment during re-replication, we performed a synchronization experiment in Geminin-depleted U2OS cells. Cells were arrested at G2/M by a sequential block with thymidine and the CDK1 inhibitor RO-3306, depleted of Geminin and then released into the next cell cycle (Supplementary Fig. 5b). To follow FANCD2 recruitment as cell progressed through S and G2 phases, cells were pulse-labelled with EdU and immunostained against FANCD2, together with the replication stress marker RPA32, and the G2/M marker pH3 (H3-Ser10Pho). While control cells showed the characteristic early, middle and late S-phase EdU patterns as cells progressed through S-phase, in Geminin-depleted cells a population with a particular diffused EdU pattern was evident from 14 h post-release, termed “R” from re-replicating (Fig. 2d). This cell population, which was actively synthesizing DNA, increased progressively and accumulated at the G2/M boundary, as shown by EdU incorporation in pH3-positive cells (Supplementary Fig. 5c). In parallel to the appearance of re-replicating cells, FANCD2 and RPA32 foci increased significantly in Geminin-depleted cells from 14 h post-release and accumulated at later time-points (Fig. 2e). Importantly, FANCD2 and RPA32 foci accumulation was evident specifically in re-replicating cells, as judged by the EdU pattern, and persisted as cells accumulated at G2/M (Supplementary Fig. 5c, d), indicating that re-replication upon Geminin loss begins within the first round of DNA synthesis and leads to early FANCD2 recruitment and RPA32 accumulation.

Next, to investigate whether FANCD2 is actively recruited at the vicinity of re-replicating forks, we pulse-labelled Geminin-depleted cells with EdU and monitored FANCD2 interaction with the newly synthesized DNA by proximity ligation assays (PLA). Geminin depletion significantly increased the number of EdU-FANCD2 PLA foci when compared to control cells (Fig. 3a). These results were also reproduced when we quantified the number of interacting PLA foci between FANCD2 and other replisome factors such as MCM2 or PCNA (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 5e). Notably, the interaction between the replisome and FANCD2 not only occurred in S-phase cells but became evident in those cells exhibiting the characteristic EdU incorporation pattern of re-replicating cells (Fig. 3b). Altogether, these results suggest that re-replication upon Geminin loss begins within the first round of DNA synthesis and induces FANCD2 recruitment to active forks prior to G2/M arrest and high levels of DNA damage.

FANCD2 limits fork progression in Geminin-depleted cells upon checkpoint activation
Given its accumulation at re-replicating forks, we next sought to determine whether FANCD2 was required to limit the extent of re-replication. Interestingly, co-depletion of Geminin and FANCD2 in U2OS cells did not increase the percentage of EdU positive cells with a DNA content >4C nor the nuclear size above that of Geminin-depleted cells, but on the contrary slightly reduced it (Fig. 3c, d). These results were also reproduced in hTERT-RPE1 cells (Supplementary Fig. 6a), excluding the possibility that FANCD2 restricts re-replication upon Geminin-depletion.

To further explore the dynamics of replication in cells depleted of Geminin and FANCD2, we then analyzed the progression of forks by DNA fiber assays. Double Geminin and FANCD2-depleted cells significantly increased fiber tract length and fork asymmetry (Fig. 3e), suggesting that FANCD2 limits fork speed and prevents fork stalling in the absence of Geminin. Although we could not measure origin distances due to DNA fiber analysis limitations, we observed that Geminin-depleted cells showed a slight increase in origin firing (Fig. 3f), according to the idea that over-licensing can also lead to ectopic origin firing32. However, downregulation of FANCD2 did not significantly alter the percentage of origin initiation (Fig. 3f), arguing against a primarily role for this protein in preventing ectopic firing of origins in the context of re-replication. Additionally, we investigated the effect of co-depleting Geminin and FANCD2 on cell cycle progression, using EdU incorporation and pH3 as markers of S and G2/M phases, respectively. According to the results obtained during synchronization experiments, Geminin depletion led to an increased proportion of cells retaining active DNA synthesis in G2, while they also exhibited high levels of DNA damage (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Fig. 6b). Geminin-depleted cells also demonstrated increased levels of phosphorylated Chk1 (Fig. 3h), in agreement with re-replication triggering checkpoint activation51–53. Indeed, inhibition of the G2/M checkpoint by incubating Geminin-depleted cells with a low dose of the VE-821 ATR inhibitor or with the general checkpoint inhibitor caffeine suppressed re-replication and the associated DNA damage phenotypes (Supplementary Fig. 6c, d). This suggests that overriding the G2/M checkpoint forces Geminin-depleted cells into mitosis prematurely, leaving insufficient time for extensive re-replication to occur. Consistent with this, incubation of Geminin-depleted cells with VE-821 resulted in the accumulation of inherited DNA lesions, as shown by increased micronuclei, aberrant mitosis, and reduced cell survival (Supplementary Fig. 6e, f). Importantly, co-depletion of Geminin and FANCD2 further increased the percentage of G2-arrested and EdU-positive cells, while it retained checkpoint activity (Fig. 3g, h), suggesting that FANCD2 is not required for checkpoint activation in response to re-replication. Collectively, these results indicate that depletion of FANCD2 accelerates fork speed and causes DNA damage upon checkpoint activation in Geminin-depleted cells.

Loss of FANCD2 promotes the accumulation of ssDNA gaps and genomic instability in Geminin-depleted cells
Unrestrained fork progression promotes the accumulation of ssDNA gaps54,55. These gaps may lead to excessive RPA loading and subsequent depletion of the available RPA pool, leading to fork breakage and genome instability56–58. To determine whether the abnormal progression of forks in double Geminin and FANCD2-depleted cells correlated with an accumulation of ssDNA gaps, we analyzed the formation of RPA foci. Depletion of Geminin and FANCD2 triggered the accumulation of RPA foci exclusively in re-replicating cells, as shown by colocalization of pre-extracted RPA32 and pH3 positive cells (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 7a). Notably, the intensity of RPA foci was also significantly increased in double-depleted cells (Supplementary Fig. 7b), likely due to longer ssDNA gaps. As an alternative way to visualize ssDNA, we also labeled the cells with the nucleotide analogue BrdU, which was then detected by immunofluorescence under native conditions. Consistent with the results observed during analysis of RPA32 foci, Geminin depletion induced the formation of BrdU foci while the proportion of cells exhibiting BrdU foci was further increased upon co-depletion with FANCD2 (Fig. 4b). To further confirm the presence of ssDNA gaps, we performed a DNA fiber assay in cells depleted of Geminin and FANCD2 and incubated with the S1 endonuclease. Labelled nascent DNA tracks were shorter and thus sensitive to the S1 enzyme in double Geminin and FANCD2-depleted cells compared to single-depleted and control cells (Fig. 4c). The shortening in tract length observed upon incubation of Geminin and FANCD2-double depleted cells to S1 nuclease was similar to that observed in cells incubated with the PARP inhibitor Olaparib (Fig. 4d). This is consistent with previous findings showing that PARPi sensitivity correlates with fork acceleration and gap formation58,59. Indeed, cells depleted of Geminin slightly increased the levels of parylation (Fig. 4d), whereas PARP inhibition in Geminin-depleted cells induced sensitivity to S1 nuclease activity and accumulation of RPA32 and BrdU foci, together with increased DSBs and reduced cell viability (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 7c-e). This reinforces the idea that an excess of ssDNA gaps underlies the high levels of genomic instability observed in re-replicating cells upon Geminin loss.

Finally, we tested whether increased formation of ssDNA gaps and accumulation of DNA damage in Geminin and FANCD2 double-depleted cells would result in chromosome breakage and high levels of genomic instability. As anticipated, metaphase spreads from Geminin-depleted cells already exhibited an increased number of chromosome breaks and aberrations (Fig. 4f). However, depletion of FANCD2 in Geminin-defective cells further exacerbated these phenotypes (Fig. 4f). Additional signatures of persistent genomic instability, such as 53BP1 nuclear bodies or micronuclei were also increased in Geminin and FANCD2 double-depleted cells across different cell lines (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 7f, g). Altogether, the results suggest that FANCD2 prevents the accumulation of ssDNA gaps and deleterious levels of DNA damage upon Geminin loss.

Contribution of FANCD2 mono-ubiquitination to cell survival during re-replication
The role of FANCD2 during replisome surveillance occurs independently of its mono-ubiquitination by the FA core complex, while it is required to preserve fork stability upon acute replication stress38,60. To explore the requirement of FANCD2 mono-ubiquitination for its function in sustaining the survival of re-replicating cells, we depleted FANCA - a key subunit of the E3 ubiquitin-ligase FA core complex - in Geminin-depleted cells. Consistent with the results obtained during chromatin fractionation, depletion of Geminin induced mono-ubiquitination of FANCD2, while depletion of FANCA reduced total FANCD2 levels (Fig. 5a), as previously described54. Our analyses also revealed increased DSBs (Fig. 5b) and accumulation of RPA foci (Fig. 5c) in double Geminin and FANCA-depleted cells in comparison to single Geminin-depleted cells. Moreover, clonogenic assays showed reduced survival of Geminin-deficient cells upon FANCA depletion (Fig. 5d), although this effect was less pronounced than that observed upon FANCD2 loss. Consistent with this partial effect, FANCD2 foci, although significantly reduced, could still be detected on chromatin in Geminin and FANCA double-depleted cells (Fig. 5e).

To further explore the contribution on FANCD2 mono-ubiquitination for survival of re-replicating cells, we evaluated the clonogenic capacity of FANCD2-KO U2OS cells reconstituted with either FANCD2-WT or the ubiquitination-resistant FANCD2-K561R mutant to Geminin depletion (Fig. 5f). As anticipated, depletion of Geminin in FANCD2-KO cells induced massive cell death (Fig. 5g) in respect to control cells. Interestingly, while introduction of FANCD2-WT significantly improved cell viability in Geminin-depleted cells, depletion of Geminin in cells expressing the FANCD2-K561R mutant showed an intermediate clonogenic outgrowth (Fig. 5g). These results are consistent with residual levels of chromatin-bound, non-ubiquitinated FANCD2 partially rescuing replication fork restart and cell proliferation upon replication stress60–62. Thus, our data indicate that FANCD2 mono-ubiquitination contributes to preserve cell survival upon re-replication and suggest an additional ubiquitination-independent role protecting genome integrity.

FANCD2 limits R-loop-associated fragility in Geminin-depleted cells
Intragenic origins mapping within highly transcribed genes have been shown to fire early during S phase upon oncogene-induced replication stress72. Furthermore, early replicating regions have been associated with transcriptionally active sites and accessible chromatin configuration73,74. Thus, we wondered whether Geminin depletion leads to fork stalling during early replication. Based on the analysis of publicly available Repli-seq datasets from the ENCODE project, which map replication timing across individual S subphases at specific genomic sites75, we observe a significant increase in BrdU intensity during early S phase, and a reduction in mid-to-late replication timing in those origins identified to accumulate FANCD2 specifically in Geminin-depleted cells when compared to control cells (Fig. 6f), suggesting these origins replicate early.

Transcriptional activity at early replicating regions has been linked to DNA damage and DNA-RNA hybrids at early replicating fragile sites (ERFSs)76,77. Thus, we analyzed the levels of DNA damage and DNA-RNA hybrids from available γH2AX ChIP-seq78 and DRIPc-seq79 data of wild-type K562 cells. γH2AX signal was higher in those genes specifically enriched in FANCD2 upon Geminin loss (Fig. 7a). In addition, and despite DNA-RNA hybrid distribution profiles were similar, these genes exhibited higher DRIPc-seq signal levels (Fig. 7b). These results suggest FANCD2 accumulation upon Geminin depletion occurs at R-loop containing regions that are prone to break even under unperturbed conditions, suggesting they could correspond to ERFSs. By lifting over ERFS data from synchronized mouse B cells76 employing the LiftOver (UCSC) alignment tool, we analyzed FANCD2 coverage over potential human ERFSs. Strikingly, metagenomic analyses showed a significant accumulation of FANCD2 at ERFSs in Geminin-depleted cells (Fig. 7c). Altogether, these results suggest that re-replication upon Geminin loss leads to the expression of ERFSs, supporting a model in which active transcription and R-loops cause fork stalling close to early replicating regions, thus contributing to genome instability. To test this hypothesis, we used the adenosine analog Cordycepin and we over-expressed RNaseH1 to examine the effect of inhibiting general transcription or degrading DNA-RNA hybrids in replication fork stalling (FANCD2 foci), ssDNA gaps (RPA foci) and DSBs (γH2AX foci) upon Geminin depletion. Cordycepin treatment effectively reduced EU incorporation (Supplementary Fig. 8f), supporting its role as a general transcription inhibitor. However, we were able to observe that it also caused a reduction in EdU incorporation (Supplementary Fig. 8g), which could partially impact S-phase progression. This was not the case for cells over-expressing RNaseH1, where bulk EdU incorporation remained unaffected (Supplementary Fig. 8g). Importantly, both treatment with Cordycepin and RNaseH1 over-expression significantly reduced the number of γH2AX, FANCD2 and RPA foci of Geminin-depleted cells (Fig. 7d, e). These results support that aberrant origin licensing and re-replication upon Geminin loss promote fragility of ERFSs, which is prevented by FANCD2 recruitment.
